name: Lithium aluminium hydride
typicalUses: Reduces esters, carboxylic acids and aldehydes/ketones to alcohols
Reduces amides and nitriles to amines
Opens epoxides at the less hindered carbon
chemoselectivity: Reduces almost every C=O group: aldehydes, ketones, esters, acids, acid chlorides, amides (to amines)
Reduces nitriles to primary amines and azides to amines
Leaves isolated C=C and C≡C bonds alone
pitfalls: Reacts violently with water and alcohols (H₂ evolves): use dry ether or THF and a careful workup
A carboxylic acid is first deprotonated (one hydride lost as H₂) before it is reduced to the primary alcohol
Amides give amines, not alcohols

name: Sodium borohydride
typicalUses: Reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols, usually in MeOH or EtOH at 0 °C to room temperature
With CeCl₃ (Luche conditions): 1,2-reduction of enones to allylic alcohols
chemoselectivity: Reduces aldehydes, ketones and acyl chlorides
Does not reduce esters, amides, carboxylic acids or nitriles under normal conditions
Leaves isolated C=C bonds alone
pitfalls: It delivers H⁻ to carbon; it is not used as a base
Decomposes in acid with H₂ evolution and slowly reacts with protic solvents
Without CeCl₃, enones can undergo some 1,4-(conjugate) reduction

name: Diisobutylaluminium hydride
typicalUses: Ester → aldehyde with 1 equivalent at −78 °C
Nitrile → aldehyde after aqueous workup (via the aluminium imine)
Lactone → lactol
chemoselectivity: At −78 °C the tetrahedral intermediate from an ester is stable, so the aldehyde is only released on workup
With excess reagent or on warming, esters are reduced further to primary alcohols
Nitriles stop at the imine stage, which hydrolyses to the aldehyde
Not the usual reagent for azides: use H₂/Pd, LiAlH₄ or PPh₃/H₂O (Staudinger)
pitfalls: Aluminium is Lewis acidic: DIBAL-H coordinates the carbonyl oxygen before delivering hydride
Warming before the quench over-reduces esters to alcohols
todoVerify: Behaviour of DIBAL-H towards organic azides: treated here as not a standard method

name: L-Selectride
typicalUses: Diastereoselective reduction of cyclic ketones from the less hindered face
Conjugate (1,4) reduction of some enones
chemoselectivity: Very bulky: delivers hydride equatorially, so 4-tert-butylcyclohexanone gives mainly the axial (cis) alcohol
Small hydrides (NaBH₄, LiAlH₄) give mainly the equatorial (trans) alcohol from the same ketone
pitfalls: Opposite diastereoselectivity to NaBH₄ on unhindered cyclohexanones
Moisture- and air-sensitive; oxidative workup (H₂O₂/NaOH) removes the boron by-products
todoVerify: Extent of 1,4-reduction of enones by L-Selectride (substrate-dependent)

name: Sodium cyanoborohydride
typicalUses: Reductive amination (Borch) at pH ≈ 6–7
chemoselectivity: The electron-withdrawing CN makes it much weaker than NaBH₄ and stable in mildly acidic solution
At pH 6–7 it reduces iminium ions much faster than aldehydes or ketones
pitfalls: Strong acid releases HCN, which is highly toxic
Too low a pH protonates the amine and stops imine formation

name: Sodium triacetoxyborohydride
typicalUses: Reductive amination of aldehydes and ketones, often in 1,2-dichloroethane with AcOH
chemoselectivity: Reduces iminium ions quickly, aldehydes slowly and ketones very slowly
A milder, less toxic alternative to NaBH₃CN
pitfalls: Decomposed by methanol and water: use aprotic solvents
Not a general carbonyl reducing agent

name: Borane–THF
typicalUses: Hydroboration of alkenes (then H₂O₂/NaOH → anti-Markovnikov alcohol, syn addition)
Selective reduction of carboxylic acids to primary alcohols
chemoselectivity: Reduces carboxylic acids faster than esters: the opposite selectivity to NaBH₄
Electrophilic: it adds to C=C with B going to the less substituted carbon
pitfalls: BH₃ is a Lewis acid stabilised by THF (or Me₂S) as a donor
Hydroboration is syn; the subsequent oxidation proceeds with retention

name: Sodium in liquid ammonia
typicalUses: Alkyne → (E)-alkene (anti addition of H)
Birch reduction of arenes to 1,4-cyclohexadienes (with an alcohol as proton source)
chemoselectivity: Leaves isolated alkenes alone
Arenes with electron-donating groups (e.g. OMe) keep the substituent on a remaining C=C; electron-withdrawing groups end up on an sp³ carbon
pitfalls: Gives the E-alkene, the opposite of Lindlar hydrogenation
Lithium is often used instead of sodium

name: Hydrogen over palladium on carbon
typicalUses: Hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes to alkanes
Nitro groups to amines
Removal of benzyl ethers and Cbz groups by hydrogenolysis
chemoselectivity: Syn addition of H₂ from the less hindered face
Benzene rings, esters and most ketones are untouched under mild conditions
Aryl halides can be dehalogenated
pitfalls: Cannot stop at the alkene from an alkyne: use Lindlar's catalyst
Benzyl protecting groups are removed too

name: Lindlar's catalyst with hydrogen
typicalUses: Alkyne → (Z)-alkene
chemoselectivity: The poisoned catalyst stops at the alkene
Reduces alkynes much faster than alkenes already present
pitfalls: Syn addition gives the Z-alkene; use Na/NH₃ for the E-alkene

name: Zinc amalgam and hydrochloric acid
typicalUses: Clemmensen reduction: aryl ketone C=O → CH₂ (e.g. after Friedel–Crafts acylation)
chemoselectivity: Strongly acidic: acid-sensitive groups (acetals, tertiary alcohols) do not survive
pitfalls: Complementary to the Wolff–Kishner reduction, which works under strongly basic conditions

name: Hydrazine and KOH (Wolff–Kishner)
typicalUses: Wolff–Kishner reduction: C=O → CH₂ via the hydrazone, with loss of N₂
chemoselectivity: Strongly basic and hot: esters are hydrolysed, base-sensitive groups suffer
pitfalls: Hydrazine first acts as a nucleophile (forming the hydrazone); the reduction follows on heating with base

name: Tin(II) chloride with HCl
typicalUses: Reduction of aromatic nitro groups to anilines
chemoselectivity: Chemoselective for NO₂: leaves ketones, esters and nitriles alone
Fe/HCl or Zn/HCl do the same job
pitfalls: The aniline is obtained as its ammonium salt; basify to isolate the free amine
